title: Standing for justice
hook: help your brother, oppressor or oppressed: how do you help an oppressor?
tomorrow: is saying it out loud always the brave thing?

segments.voice: Yesterday: feed people, a plate set between a greeting and a prayer. Today's saying is even shorter, and much stranger.

A group chat turns on someone. Screenshots, crying-laughing faces, one person leading it, and that person is your friend. Loyalty says back your friend. Fairness says the other kid is getting flattened. Then a saying of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ seems to make it harder: help your brother, whether he is the one doing wrong or the one being wronged. Help the one doing wrong? That's the odd part. The people listening thought so too, and one of them asked.
screen: `THE CHAT TURNS ON SOMEONE.` → `LOYALTY OR FAIRNESS?` → `HELP THE ONE DOING WRONG?`

segments.voice: Here's the question, in Sahih al-Bukhari. Messenger of God, we can help him when he's wronged. But how do we help him when he's the one doing wrong? The answer solves the puzzle. In one report: stop him; that is your help to him. In another: take hold of his hand. Read it twice and loyalty flips over. Helping a friend doesn't mean backing whatever he does. When he's the one doing harm, the loyal move is to take his hand off the other person. That helps two people at once: the one being hurt, and the one about to carry the wrong. The Qur'an presses it further. In Pickthall's words: "Be ye staunch in justice, witnesses for Allah, even though it be against yourselves or (your) parents or (your) kindred." Yourself. Your parents. Your own family. Justice doesn't come with a family discount. And notice what the hadith never says. It doesn't say drop your friend. It still calls him your brother, even mid-wrong. The help changes shape; the bond stays. One to tell someone tonight: in this hadith, stopping a friend who's in the wrong still goes by the name help.
screen: `HOW DO WE HELP THE ONE DOING WRONG?` · `STOP HIM. TAKE HOLD OF HIS HAND.` · `EVEN AGAINST YOURSELF OR YOUR KIN.` · `STILL YOUR BROTHER.` · then, large: `STOP THE OPPRESSOR.`

segments.voice: Hold one hand out, palm forward, the way you'd stop someone gently: not a shove, a pause. Keep it there, breathing slowly, and bring to mind one wrong you've watched happen lately, small or large. Ask whose hand you might have held, and how kindly. When you're ready, let the hand rest in your lap.
screen: `PALM OUT: A PAUSE, NOT A SHOVE.` · `ONE WRONG YOU'VE WATCHED.` · `WHOSE HAND, AND HOW KINDLY?`

segments.voice: Standing for justice: stopping a wrong, even when the one doing it is your own. In the hadith, stopping him is helping him.
Hold onto this: stop the oppressor, and you've helped him as well as the one he hurt. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1738 COUNTS.` → `SERVICE AND JUSTICE · 3 OF 10.` → `TOMORROW: IS SAYING IT OUT LOUD ALWAYS BRAVE?`

howItsDone: Muslims quote this hadith when a friend, relative or their own community is in the wrong: standing with them means stopping the harm, not covering for it.
